(2)

(2)

questions.question_text:
A firework rocket starts from rest at ground level and moves vertically. In the first 3 s of its motion, the rocket rises 27 m. The rocket is modelled as a particle moving with constant acceleration $a\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Find
(a) the value of $a$,
(2)
(b) the speed of the rocket 3 s after it has left the ground.
(2)
After 3 s, the rocket burns out. The motion of the rocket is now modelled as that of a particle moving freely under gravity.
(c) Find the height of the rocket above the ground 5 s after it has left the ground.
(4)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) $27 = 0 + \frac{1}{2}a(3)^2 \Rightarrow a = 6$
M1 A1 (2)
(b) $v = 6\times 3 = 18\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
M1 A1 f.t. (2)
(c) From $t=3$ to $t=5$, $s = 18\times 2 - \frac{1}{2}\times 9.8\times 2^2$
M1 A1 f.t.
Total ht. $= s+27 = 43.4\,\text{m},\ 43\,\text{m}$
M1 A1 (4)

questions.stem: A car moves along a horizontal straight road, passing two points $A$ and $B$. At $A$ the speed of the car is $15\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. When the driver passes $A$, he sees a warning sign $W$ ahead of him, $120\,\text{m}$ away. He immediately applies the brakes and the car decelerates with uniform deceleration, reaching $W$ with speed $5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. At $W$, the driver sees that the road is clear. He then immediately accelerates the car with uniform acceleration for 16 s to reach a speed of $V\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ ($V > 15$). He then maintains the car at a constant speed of $V\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Moving at this constant speed, the car passes $B$ after a further 22 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Sketch, in the space below, a speed-time graph to illustrate the motion of the car as it moves from $A$ to $B$.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) Shape 'V' from 15 down to 5 then up to $V$
B1
Shape for last 22 s (with $V > 15$)
B1
Correct labelling (15, 5, 16, 22 shown)
B1 (3)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Find the time taken for the car to move from $A$ to $W$.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) $\frac{1}{2}(15+5)\times t = 120$
M1
$\Rightarrow t = 12 \Rightarrow T = 12+16+22 = 50\,\text{s}$
M1 A1 (3)

parts.label: c
parts.text:
The distance from $A$ to $B$ is 1 km.

(c) Find the value of $V$.
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) $120 + \frac{1}{2}(V+5)\times 16 + 22V = 1000$
M1 B1 A1
Solve: $30V = 840 \Rightarrow V = 28$
DM1 A1 (5)

questions.notes: Part (b) as printed asks for the time taken for the car to move from A to B (the whole journey), reusing the value t found in the working; mark scheme's t=12 refers to the deceleration phase, then total T=50.

(a) Sketch, in the space below, a speed-time graph to illustrate the motion of the car as it moves from $A$ to $B$.
(3)

questions.stem:
Figure 1

A particle $P$ of mass 6 kg lies on the surface of a smooth plane. The plane is inclined at an angle of $30^\circ$ to the horizontal. The particle is held in equilibrium by a force of magnitude $49\,\text{N}$, acting at an angle $\theta$ to the plane, as shown in Figure 1. The force acts in a vertical plane through a line of greatest slope of the plane.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Show that $\cos\theta = \frac{3}{5}$.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) R (// plane): $49\cos\theta = 6g\sin 30$
M1 A1
$\Rightarrow \cos\theta = 3/5\ *$
A1 (3)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Find the normal reaction between $P$ and the plane.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) R (perp to plane): $R = 6g\cos 30 + 49\sin\theta$
M1 A1
$R \approx 90.1$ or $90\,\text{N}$
DM1 A1 (4)

parts.label: c
parts.text:
The direction of the force of magnitude $49\,\text{N}$ is now changed. It is now applied horizontally to $P$ so that $P$ moves up the plane. The force again acts in a vertical plane through a line of greatest slope of the plane.

(c) Find the initial acceleration of $P$.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) R (// to plane): $49\cos 30 - 6g\sin 30 = 6a$
M1 A2,1,0
$\Rightarrow a \approx 2.17$ or $2.2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$
A1 (4)

Figure 1

A particle $P$ of mass 6 kg lies on the surface of a smooth plane. The plane is inclined at an angle of $30^\circ$ to the horizontal. The particle is held in equilibrium by a force of magnitude $49\,\text{N}$, acting at an angle $\theta$ to the plane, as shown in Figure 1. The force acts in a vertical plane through a line of greatest slope of the plane.
(a) Show that $\cos\theta = \frac{3}{5}$.
(3)
(b) Find the normal reaction between $P$ and the plane.
(4)
The direction of the force of magnitude $49\,\text{N}$ is now changed. It is now applied horizontally to $P$ so that $P$ moves up the plane. The force again acts in a vertical plane through a line of greatest slope of the plane.

(c) Find the initial acceleration of $P$.
(4)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) R (// plane): $49\cos\theta = 6g\sin 30$
M1 A1
$\Rightarrow \cos\theta = 3/5\ *$
A1 (3)
(b) R (perp to plane): $R = 6g\cos 30 + 49\sin\theta$
M1 A1
$R \approx 90.1$ or $90\,\text{N}$
DM1 A1 (4)
(c) R (// to plane): $49\cos 30 - 6g\sin 30 = 6a$
M1 A2,1,0
$\Rightarrow a \approx 2.17$ or $2.2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$
A1 (4)

questions.stem:
Figure 2

A beam $AB$ has mass 12 kg and length 5 m. It is held in equilibrium in a horizontal position by two vertical ropes attached to the beam. One rope is attached to $A$, the other to the point $C$ on the beam, where $BC = 1\,\text{m}$, as shown in Figure 2. The beam is modelled as a uniform rod, and the ropes as light strings.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find
(i) the tension in the rope at $C$,
(ii) the tension in the rope at $A$.
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) M($A$): $T\times 4 = 12g\times 2.5$
M1 A1
$T = 7.5g$ or $73.5\,\text{N}$
A1
R($\uparrow$) $S+T = 12g$
M1
$\Rightarrow S = 4.5g$ or $44.1\,\text{N}$
A1 (5)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
A small load of mass 16 kg is attached to the beam at a point which is $y$ metres from $A$. The load is modelled as a particle. Given that the beam remains in equilibrium in a horizontal position,

(b) find, in terms of $y$, an expression for the tension in the rope at $C$.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) M($A$) $V\times 4 = 16g\times y + 12g\times 2.5$
M1 A1
$V = 4gy + 7.5g$ or $39.2y + 73.5\,\text{N}$
A1 (3)

parts.label: c
parts.text:
The rope at $C$ will break if its tension exceeds $98\,\text{N}$. The rope at $A$ cannot break.

(c) Find the range of possible positions on the beam where the load can be attached without the rope at $C$ breaking.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) $V \leqslant 98 \Rightarrow 39.2y + 73.5 \leqslant 98$
M1
$\Rightarrow y \leqslant 0.625 = 5/8$
DM1
Hence "load must be no more than 5/8 m from $A$" (o.e.)
A1 (3)

questions.stem:
[In this question, the unit vectors $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ are due east and due north respectively.]

A particle $P$ is moving with constant velocity $(-5\mathbf{i}+8\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Find

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) the speed of $P$,
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) Speed $= \sqrt{5^2+8^2} \approx 9.43\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
M1 A1 (2)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) the direction of motion of $P$, giving your answer as a bearing.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) Forming $\arctan\frac{8}{5}$ or $\arctan\frac{5}{8}$ oe
M1
Bearing $= 360-\arctan\frac{5}{8}$ or $270+\arctan\frac{8}{5} = 328$
DM1 A1 (3)

parts.label: c
parts.text:
At time $t=0$, $P$ is at the point $A$ with position vector $(7\mathbf{i}-10\mathbf{j})\,\text{m}$ relative to a fixed origin $O$. When $t=3\,\text{s}$, the velocity of $P$ changes and it moves with velocity $(u\mathbf{i}+v\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, where $u$ and $v$ are constants. After a further 4 s, it passes through $O$ and continues to move with velocity $(u\mathbf{i}+v\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
(c) Find the values of $u$ and $v$.
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) At $t=3$, p.v. of $P = (7-15)\mathbf{i}+(-10+24)\mathbf{j} = -8\mathbf{i}+14\mathbf{j}$
M1 A1
Hence $-8\mathbf{i}+14\mathbf{j}+4(u\mathbf{i}+v\mathbf{j}) = \mathbf{0}$
M1
$\Rightarrow u=2,\ v=-3.5$
DM1 A1 (5)

parts.label: d
parts.text:
(d) Find the total time taken for $P$ to move from $A$ to a position which is due south of $A$.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) p.v. of $P$ $t$ secs after changing course $= (-8\mathbf{i}+14\mathbf{j})+t(2\mathbf{i}-3.5\mathbf{j})$
M1
$=7\mathbf{i}+\ldots$
DM1
Hence total time $= 10.5\,\text{s}$
A1 (3)

questions.stem:
Figure 3

Two particles $A$ and $B$, of mass $m$ and $2m$ respectively, are attached to the ends of a light inextensible string. The particle $A$ lies on a rough horizontal table. The string passes over a small smooth pulley $P$ fixed on the edge of the table. The particle $B$ hangs freely below the pulley, as shown in Figure 3. The coefficient of friction between $A$ and the table is $\mu$. The particles are released from rest with the string taut. Immediately after release, the magnitude of the acceleration of $A$ and $B$ is $\frac{4}{9}g$. By writing down separate equations of motion for $A$ and $B$,

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) find the tension in the string immediately after the particles begin to move,
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) $B$: $2mg - T = 2m\times \frac{4}{9}g$
M1 A1
$\Rightarrow T = \frac{10mg}{9}$
A1 (3)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) show that $\mu = \frac{2}{3}$.
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) $A$: $T - \mu mg = m\times \frac{4}{9}g$
M1 B1 A1
Sub for $T$ and solve: $\mu = 2/3\ *$
DM1 A1 (5)

parts.label: c
parts.text:
When $B$ has fallen a distance $h$, it hits the ground and does not rebound. Particle $A$ is then a distance $\frac{1}{3}h$ from $P$.

(c) Find the speed of $A$ as it reaches $P$.
(6)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) When $B$ hits: $v^2 = 2\times \frac{4}{9}g\times h$
M1 A1
Deceleration of $A$ after $B$ hits: $ma = \mu mg \Rightarrow a = \frac{2}{3}g$
M1 A1 f.t.
Speed of $A$ at $P$: $V^2 = \frac{8gh}{9} - 2\times\frac{2g}{3}\times \frac{h}{3}$
DM1
$\Rightarrow V = \frac{2}{3}\sqrt{gh}$
A1 (6)

parts.label: d
parts.text:
(d) State how you have used the information that the string is light.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) Same tension on $A$ and $B$
B1 (1)
